description: I am Afreen Navas, an engineering student passionate about space and exploring new ideas. Through this challenge, I hope to uncover the traces of humanity left behind as we venture into new frontiers. Every piece of equipment represents a mission, a scientific purpose, and a part of our journey into the unknown. I aim to tell these stories meaningfully, combining creativity, scientific curiosity, and a desire to look beyond what meets the eye.
summary:
Our Project Summary 

Inspired by NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 problem statement, “Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Storytelling About the Discarded Equipment on Mars and the Moon,” our project "Past Finders" explores the stories behind equipment left behind during space missions. Rather than viewing these objects as mere remnants, we wanted to highlight the scientific purpose, challenges and history associated with each one.

We developed "Abandoned, But Not Forgotten", an interactive, browser-based exploration game featuring four playable levels across Earth, the Moon and Mars. Players navigate environments, interact with abandoned equipment, solve puzzles and unlock mission files that reveal stories based on real missions, including Surveyor 3 and Phoenix.

The game was developed collaboratively using HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the front end, with Python and Flask powering the backend. JSON-based mission data, interactive gameplay mechanics, player accounts and progress tracking bring the experience together. The application was deployed online using Render and tested by multiple players.

Through this project, we aim to transform space history into an engaging experience, reminding players that even when a mission ends, its discoveries and legacy remain.
details:
Project Details – Abandoned, But Not Forgotten "PAST FINDERS-Abandoned, But Not Forgotten" is an interactive exploration game developed in response to the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 problem statement, “Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Storytelling About the Discarded Equipment on Mars and the Moon.” The project aims to bring attention to the scientific equipments left behind during space exploration and the missions, discoveries and challenges associated with them. Instead of presenting these objects through conventional information panels, we wanted players to experience their stories through exploration and gameplay. The game takes players through four levels, beginning at an Earth-based control station and progressing to the Moon and Mars. Players interact with their surroundings, locate abandoned equipment, collect clues and solve challenges to advance. These include tuning an unknown radio signal which takes the player to the space to locate it's source, restoring power to the Surveyor 3 lander by connecting a circuit, and comparing images of the Phoenix landing site to the destroyed image of the lander to identify changes. As players progress, they unlock Mission Files containing factual information about real missions, including Surveyor 3, Apollo 12 and Phoenix. Fictional narrative elements are clearly distinguished from historical facts. The game combines education with interactive entertainment, making space history more engaging and accessible. It encourages curiosity about planetary exploration while helping players understand the scientific purpose and legacy of equipment that remains on other worlds. Our intended impact is to shift the perception of abandoned equipment from forgotten debris to valuable traces of human exploration. We developed the game using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with JavaScript Canvas for the game environment and Web Audio for procedural sound effects. Python and Flask power the backend, while SQLite manages player accounts and saved progress. Mission information is organised using JSON. The application was deployed using Render. Our creative approach lies in turning historical mission information into an interactive journey rather than simply retelling it. We considered scientific accuracy, the distinction between fact and fiction, gameplay progression, puzzle difficulty, usability across desktop and mobile devices, and player engagement. The project was developed collaboratively by our six-member team, with three members directly involved in coding, and tested by multiple players.

We deliberately adopted a familiar, game-oriented exploration format to make the experience more approachable and appealing to younger audiences, particularly school students. By incorporating interactive environments, puzzles, exploration and progressive level unlocking, we aim to introduce space exploration and mission history in a format that feels engaging rather than purely academic. This approach allows us to reach beyond audiences already interested in space science and encourage younger players to explore it through curiosity and play.

Ultimately, we want players to leave with one thought: a mission may end, but its contribution to exploration does not.

With hope to make more people interested in the human touch behind the space exploration through decades, this is Team Past Finders - Afreen Navas, Agriya SR, Aksa Das, Athira J Nair, Navneet Chandran, and Swathy Sathyan.
